newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign fund seen damaging for Gazprom ADS.
newsitem.headline: Foreign fund seen damaging for Gazprom ADS.

text.p: Russia's natural gas monopoly Gazprom may see its American Depositary Share programme damaged by a new fund to be backed by cheaper domestic Gazprom shares, traders and equity analysts said on Wednesday.

The issue by the fund threatens the 400 percent premium at which RAO Gazprom ADSs trade over local Russian shares, a premium based largely on the difficulty of buying and trading local shares in the world's largest natural gas company.
"If this deal comes through it will not only undermine the present ADS but jeopardise the price of future ADSs," said one senior Western trader.
"The premium is only justifiable if there is no other way to get access to underlying shares."

Shares on the Russian Trading System closed at $0.484 on Wednesday after $0.477 at Tuesday's close. Gazprom's ADS, backed by 10 underlying shares, traded at $19.92 in London at 1600 GMT, up from $19.45 on Tuesday.
Gazprom launched the ADS in October 1996, raising $430 million amid great fanfare as it touted the instrument as a unique way for foreigners to invest in the company.
Gazprom on Tuesday asked Cayman Islands-based Regent GAZ Investment Company to suspend placing paper backed by Russian Gazprom shares.

The Regent GAZ fund would be managed by Regent Fund Management in Hong Kong, part of the Regent Pacific Group, a spokesman for the group said. Regent European Securities, a Moscow broker, is also a group subsidiary.
Gazprom said Regent intended to complete a subscription for its own shares backed by $200 million worth of Gazprom shares bought by Regent subsidiaries or units on the Russian market.
But a Gazprom spokesman said the issue might face legal problems in Russia, which restricts foreign ownership of the strategic company to nine percent.
Gazprom, Russia's largest company, also said it did not approve of the plan.

"Gazprom management considers such transactions contradict Gazprom policies on dividing Gazprom shares between the domestic and foreign markets and are incompatible with Gazprom's strategy of issuing its shares in the form of American Depositary Receipts," said Eduard Ivanov, head of Gazprom's securities section.
But traders and lawyers said the fund appeared to be legal.
Baker & McKenzie securities attorney Peter Malyshev said foreign companies could avoid Russian company charter restrictions on stock ownership by establishing wholly owned Russian subsidiaries.
"Wholly owned subsidiaries, because they are Russian-registered entities, do not face these restrictions and as such can and do buy as many shares as they want," he said.
Traders say they can sell Gazprom shares to anyone in Russia after offering the company right of first refusal to buy.
"Once you have bought the shares there are no restrictions whatsoever," said Alexander Babian, Director of Strategic Investment at CentreInvest Securities in Moscow.

Babian estimated that close to 50 percent of Gazprom shares traded in Russia are already bought with foreign money through locally-owned subsidiaries. Another senior trader said foreign turnover was closer to one quarter of local sales.
The Regent GAZ fund, at $200 million, is about one-third the market capitalisation of the ADS plan, Babian said, but he estimated the total market cap for the company was about $13 billion.
But it could be a good start. "Regent is someone who will be believed," Babian said. "It was a good idea."
